chunks.source: NParks Singapore FloraFaunaWeb — Licuala spinosa (Mangrove Fan Palm)
chunks.text: Licuala spinosa, commonly called the mangrove fan palm, spiny licuala or (in some trade contexts) 'good luck palm', is a densely clumping, multi-stemmed palm that sends up numerous slender stems from a shared base rather than growing as a single trunk, typically reaching around 3-4 m in cultivation (other sources report a wider possible range of roughly 2-7 m), each stem topped with a crown of about 15-17 distinctive fan-shaped (costapalmate) leaves. Its species name and the 'spiny' common name both refer to the rows of small, sharp spines that line its leaf stalks (petioles), a defensive feature that also makes careful handling necessary when planting or pruning it. Native across a broad swath of South and Southeast Asia — from Bangladesh through the Indochinese peninsula, Malaysia and Indonesia to the Philippines — it is characteristically a plant of brackish, waterlogged coastal habitats: mangrove swamp margins, tidal riverbanks and similar lowland wetland forest edges, which is the direct source of its common name and explains its strong tolerance of wet, poorly drained soil in cultivated settings. In gardens it is valued mainly as a lush, architecturally striking understorey or clumping accent palm for tropical landscaping, particularly in damp or poorly drained spots where many other ornamentals would struggle.

This Philippine ethnobotanical reference, compiling traditional Southeast Asian uses of the species known locally as balabat, documents a range of everyday practical and traditional-medicine applications beyond its ornamental garden role: in Cambodia its fan-shaped leaves are woven into hats and used as food-wrapping material, much as banana or other large palm leaves are used elsewhere in the region, while the tender heart and terminal growing bud of the palm are harvested and cooked as a vegetable (a 'palm heart'-style use shared with several other clustering palms). In traditional Cambodian medicine, preparations from its roots are combined into compound remedies, and the bark of the trunk has reportedly been used in traditional treatment of tuberculosis — claims that, as with most historical ethnobotanical records of this kind, reflect long-standing folk practice rather than clinically validated modern medical treatment, and should be reported to users only as traditional use rather than endorsed remedies. Overall the species is a good example of a plant that serves triple duty in its native range — as a wetland/mangrove-margin ecological component, a source of everyday craft and food-wrapping material, and a minor component of traditional medicine — well before it became known internationally purely as an ornamental palm.
